summaries.example: Imagine saying, “Every dog is barking.” Logic asks what the words mean, what they point to, and whether the sentence follows from other sentences. Albert also studied motion. He might ask whether a moving ball keeps moving because of a force it received, and how its speed changes.
summaries.summary: Albert of Saxony was a scholar of the later Middle Ages. He studied at Paris and later helped found the University of Vienna, becoming its first rector. He also became a bishop. His most important work was in logic and natural philosophy. In logic, he studied the meanings of words, the ways terms refer, truth, difficult sentences, and consequences. A consequence is a connection in which the truth of one statement requires the truth of another. In natural philosophy, he investigated motion, quantity, the vacuum, celestial bodies, and other natural questions. He sometimes agreed with thinkers such as William of Ockham, John Buridan, and William Heytesbury, but he also changed or challenged their ideas. His writings, especially his works on logic and Aristotle's physics, were widely read and helped carry Parisian ideas into Italy and central Europe.
key_ideas: Albert of Saxony was a fourteenth-century scholar who worked mainly on logic and the study of nature.
He examined how words refer to things and how sentences can be true or false.
He developed a systematic account of consequences, or ways that statements support other statements.
In natural philosophy, he studied motion, space, the vacuum, the heavens, and mathematical questions.
His books helped spread ideas from Paris to Italy and central Europe.
summaries.why_it_matters: Albert shows that philosophy in the Middle Ages was not only about religion. Scholars carefully analyzed language, arguments, mathematics, and the natural world. His work also shows how knowledge grows through discussion: he learned from earlier thinkers, disagreed with some of them, and developed new explanations that influenced later readers.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of studying sentences, meanings, and whether one statement follows from others.
The study of nature, including bodies, motion, space, and changes in the world.
What a word or sentence points to or represents.
A rule about when one statement must be true if another statement is true.
A force or quality that Albert used to help explain why a moving body continues to move.

questions_to_think_about: How can the same word mean different things in different sentences?
What makes one statement follow from another?
Can we imagine something that could not happen naturally?
Why might studying motion require both observation and careful reasoning?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence “A person's donkey is running.” The grammatical subject appears to be “a person's donkey,” but Albert analyzes “person” as the logical subject in this kind of construction. This illustrates a larger question in medieval semantics: should logical analysis follow the sentence's visible grammar, or should it identify the term that structures its reference? Albert's answer differed from John Buridan's.
summaries.summary: Albert of Saxony was a fourteenth-century master of arts at Paris, the first rector of the University of Vienna, and later bishop of Halberstadt. The SEP entry presents him chiefly as a logician and natural philosopher. His Perutilis logica organizes medieval logical investigations into six treatises, covering propositions, term properties, truth conditions, consequences, fallacies, and insolubles and obligations. Albert generally works within an Ockhamist framework: signs and universals are understood through language or concepts, and terms refer through theories of supposition. Yet he is not merely repeating Ockham. He gives an original account of relations as the result of a comparing act of the soul, analyzes verbs such as “believe” and “know” through appellation of form, and assigns propositions their own mode of signification while avoiding treating that mode as a separate thing. His account of consequences is especially important because it unifies syllogistic reasoning and conversion within a broader theory of inference. In natural philosophy, Albert examines motion, quantity, condensation, rarefaction, the vacuum, celestial motion, and mathematical proportions. He accepts an impetus-like explanation of motion while describing it as an impressed or motive force. His works helped transmit Parisian physics and logic through Italy and central Europe.
key_ideas: Albert's Logica is a systematic six-part treatment of propositions, term properties, truth, consequences, fallacies, and paradoxes or obligations.
His semantics is strongly influenced by Ockham, but he develops independent positions on relations, propositional attitudes, complex subjects, and the signification of propositions.
He restores a version of simple supposition, unlike Buridan, and treats relations as arising through an act of the soul that compares entities.
His theory of consequences distinguishes formal from material consequences and integrates syllogistic reasoning into a broader account of inference.
Albert combines a nominalist account of language and categories with realism about knowledge of the natural world.
In physics, he considers imaginary cases such as a vacuum but insists that natural philosophy must explain the ordinary natural order.
summaries.why_it_matters: Albert's work matters because it connects several major developments in late-medieval philosophy: increasingly precise semantic analysis, systematic theories of inference, and mathematical approaches to motion. His disagreements with Ockham, Buridan, and other contemporaries show that medieval philosophy involved active debate rather than a single uniform school. His influence also demonstrates how texts can reshape intellectual traditions when they are taught, copied, and read in new regions.

important_terms.definition: The medieval study of valid reasoning, sentence structure, meaning, and the relation between language and thought.
The relation by which a term or proposition represents or refers to something.
A theory about what a term refers to in a particular proposition or use.
A relation in which the truth of the antecedent makes it impossible for the consequent to be false.
A quality or impressed force used to explain how a moving body continues its motion.
The view that universals are signs or concepts rather than independently existing things.
The study of nature, especially bodies, motion, change, space, and celestial phenomena.
A proposition that produces a paradox by appearing to say of itself that it is true or false.

questions_to_think_about: Should the logical subject of a sentence always be the same as its grammatical subject?
Can a proposition signify something in addition to what its individual terms signify?
What is gained by distinguishing formal from material consequence?
How should philosophy treat a possibility that can be imagined but cannot occur in nature?
Does borrowing ideas from several thinkers make a philosopher an eclectic compiler, or can it support originality?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “I know that the team won.” The sentence after “know” is not being used in exactly the same way as a simple description. Albert studied such sentences by asking how the form of the embedded statement is being referred to. He also used careful distinctions about meaning to handle sentences that seem to create puzzles, such as a statement that says of itself that it is false.
summaries.summary: Albert of Saxony lived in the fourteenth century. He studied and taught at Paris, became the first rector of the University of Vienna, and later served as bishop of Halberstadt. The entry focuses on his contributions to logic and natural philosophy rather than on theology. His chief logical work, the Perutilis logica, is arranged as a broad handbook. It discusses the parts of propositions, the ways terms refer, conditions for truth, consequences, fallacies, and puzzles involving self-reference and special kinds of debate. Albert often follows William of Ockham's approach, especially in treating universals as signs or concepts, but he also disagrees with John Buridan and other scholars. For example, he gives his own account of relations and of statements connected with believing and knowing. He defines a consequence as a connection in which the first statement cannot be true without the second one. In natural philosophy, he studies motion, quantity, bodies, the vacuum, the heavens, earthquakes, tides, and mathematical proportions. He considers imaginary situations, including a vacuum or more than one world, but says that physics must ultimately explain the natural order. His discussions of motion include an impetus-like force and methods for studying changing speed. His books, especially his work on Aristotle's Physics, became influential in Italy and central Europe.
key_ideas: Albert was an important fourteenth-century thinker, teacher, university leader, and bishop whose main writings concern logic and natural philosophy.
His major logic textbook explains propositions, the properties of terms, truth, inference, mistakes in reasoning, and difficult self-referential statements.
He was influenced by Ockham, Buridan, Burley, and Heytesbury, but the entry emphasizes that he made original contributions rather than simply collecting their views.
Albert's theory of consequences explains when one statement follows from another and distinguishes different kinds of consequence.
In natural philosophy, he explored real and imaginary cases, such as whether a vacuum could exist, while separating what is imaginable from what occurs naturally.
His writings on physics, motion, and proportions were widely read and helped spread Parisian ideas across Italy and central Europe.
summaries.why_it_matters: Albert's career shows how universities helped ideas travel and develop. His work joins language study with questions about science: clear definitions and valid inferences can affect how people explain motion and nature. His example also reminds us that intellectual history is often a network of disagreements, revisions, and influences rather than a simple line from one famous thinker to the next.

important_terms.definition: The study of valid reasoning and how words and sentences work together.
What a word, term, or sentence represents or refers to.
The way a term refers to something within a particular statement.
A connection where the first statement cannot be true without the second statement also being true.
The idea that a moving object has an acquired force or quality that helps explain its continued motion.
A medieval approach that treats universals mainly as words or concepts rather than separate things existing on their own.
The medieval investigation of nature, including motion, matter, space, and the heavens.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a sentence inside “I know that...” need a special kind of analysis?
What is the difference between something being imaginable and being naturally possible?
How can a philosopher use another thinker's ideas while still developing an original position?
What would happen to an argument if its first statement were true but its conclusion could be false?
